4.6 Correlation between 2 continuous variables
Why does inequality vary cross-nationally?









Suppose we want to explain why some countries are more equal or less unequal than others. Here are two possible explanations:

Welfare states can contribute to lower inequalities because they redistribute incomes across different groups in the population via taxation and cash transfers. While some welfare states are more progressive than others in that a larger share of the redistribution goes from rich to poor, we hypothesize that on average the larger the size of the welfare state, measured as social expenditure, the less unequal a country will be.
Strong trade unions can contribute to lower pre-distribution inequalities, and consequently to lower post-distribution inequalities, because they have the capacity to negotiate up the wages of ordinary workers. The share of workers that are members of a trade union, or union density, is one of the key determinants of union’s power to push employers and governments to lift wages before welfare state redistribution even occurs. Thus, we hypothesize that on average the higher the union density the less unequal the country will be.
ALSO: we suspect that social expenditure and union density are positively associated!














































To measure the strength and direction of association between 2 continuous variables we use the correlation coefficient.
To calculate it we first need to measure the covariance, which is essentially the joint variance of the two variables simultaneously. In other words, how do these variables vary together which is calculated by averaging the multiplication of the errors each observation’s values for x and y relative to their means - i.e. the distance between each data point and the means of each variable x and y. Notice how similar the formula for the covariance is to that of the variance discussed in unit 3.
The formula is as follows:
\[cov(x,y)=s_{xy}=\frac{\Sigma^n_{i=1}(x_i-\bar{x})\times(y_i - \bar{y})}{n-1}\]
Graphically, we already know what variances capture









But now for the covariance we consider both variances simultaneously:









The correlation coefficient is basically a standardised covariance so that it takes values between -1 and +1 so that the association can be measured regardless on the metric of the variable (kg, m, number of years, salary in pounds, etc).
The Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) is calculated by dividing the covariance of x and y (\(s_{xy}\)) by the product of the standard deviations of x and y (\(s_x \times s_x\)):
\[corr(x,y)=\frac{s_{xy}}{s_x \times s_y}\]
The regression coefficient indicates two fundamental properties of an association:

Strength of the relationship: based on how closely aligned the data points are and indicated by how close the number is to 0 or 1. The closer to 0 the weaker the relationship, the closer to 1 the stronger the relationship between X and Y.
Sign of the relationship: based on direction of the cloud of data points (upwards, downwards, flat) and indicated by the sign of the correlation coefficient.

Graphically, this is:

4.7 Hypothesis tests for contingency tables
The main purpose of a contingency table is to display numerically the cross-classification of two or more categorical variables. In plain English, all a contingency table does is to show the number of individual observations that belong to each combination of values of two categorical variables.
The main substantive purpose of a contingency table is to describe the patterns of association between two or more categorical variables.
In this case, we will examine the association between housing tenure
Findings:

80% of homeowners said they voted in the last general election, while 20% said they didn’t.
57% of tenants said they voted in the last general election, while 43% said they didn’t.

Bivariate inference with the chi-squared test
These differences in the electoral behaviour of homeowners and tenants seem quite large, so the next step would be to ask ourselves whether they are not just the result of sampling error? To test this we
Remember that the Null Hypothesis states that there is no association between two categorical variables or, in other words, that the distribution of one variable is the same regardless of the category of the other variables. In our case, the null hypothesis is as follows:

There is no association between voting and housing tenure
The distribution of voters and non-voters will be (broadly) the same across owners and non-owners.

We can use the expected and observed values to calculate the chi-squared statistic (\(\chi^2\)). Remember that the formula is as follows:
\[\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i} \]
This means that the chi-squared statistic is equal to the sum of the squared differences between observed counts (data) and expected counts (null hypothesis) divided by the expected counts.
The larger the value of \(\chi^2\) the greater the difference between your data and what we should expect to see if there were no relationship between the two variables of interest. The second step in the chi-squared tests addresses the following question: What is the probability that the difference between observed and expected is at least as large as that captured by chi^2 if the null hypothesis were true?
To calculate what the expected values for our table under the assumption that the null hypothesis is true - i.e. that voting is independent of tenure - we draw on a fundamental notion in probability theory that says that if two events are independent, the probability of them occurring at the same time (their joint probability) is equal to the product of the probability of each event occurring separately (their marginal probabilities).
For two independent events A and B, this is formally:
\[P(\text{A} \cap \text{B}) = P(\text{A})\times P(\text{B})\]

The Pearson’s correlation coefficient (r) is calculated by dividing the covariance of x and y (\(s_{xy}\)) by the product of the standard deviations of x and y (\(s_x \times s_x\)):
\[corr(x,y)=\frac{s_{xy}}{s_x \times s_x}\]
R will do this for you (including a t-test with Ho that the correlation coefficient is 0) with this simple line:

cor.test(lfs$loghrpay, lfs$tothrs, use="complete.obs")


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

data:  lfs$loghrpay and lfs$tothrs
t = 29.875, df = 10187, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 0.2658725 0.3015800
sample estimates:
      cor 
0.2838247 


So the correlation coefficient for the association between pay and hours worked is +0.28. This indicates a positive (as hours worked increases pay also increases) but weak relation (one variable predicts the other one to a very limited extent). Notice that the p-value is also very small, so we can concluded that the correlation is significant at the 95% confidence level - it is highly unlikely that we would find a correlation of this magnitude if in the population from which the data was sampled the correlation was actually 0 (i.e. the null hypothesis).


5.3.2 Exploring bivariate associations between 2 continuous variables using a scatterplot
We can explore this association graphically, using scatterplots. Scatterplots plot each individual observation as a point on the 2 dimensional space defined by two axis that represent the levels of each one of the variables. Each point represents the scores of each observation for the variable on the horizontal or x axis and variable on the vertical or y axis.
The ggplot2 syntax should be familiar to you by now. The only difference is the geom_point shape. Since we are dealing with a very large sample, we specify a specific shape (shape=1) for the points (a circle without fill) to make the visualisation clearer:

ggplot(data=lfs, aes(y=loghrpay, x=tothrs)) +
  geom_point(shape=1) 








As we can see as the number of hours worked increases, the pay per hour also increases, but it is a neither very steep nor strong pattern. You can tell that it is not strong by the fact that the cloud of points is quite scattered - i.e. that for any number of working hours there is quite a spread in the amounts of pay our respondents receive. In other words, total hours worked does not predict very well the pay one is going to get, so there are many other factors that must be playing a role in determining pay. This is consistent with what the weak positive correlation coefficient (r=0.29) was showing.
We can also fit in a regression line to summarise the pattern of data points. We do this by introducing the geom_smooth() function and the linear model method option.

ggplot(data=lfs, aes(y=loghrpay, x=tothrs)) +
  geom_point(shape=1) + geom_smooth(method="lm") 








The line has a positive or upward slope indicating that on average as total hour increases, average pay per hour also increases. Notice however how far the points are from the line on average, suggesting that total hours is only a weak predictor of hourly pay.

title: 5  Linear Regression
text:
5.4 Simple linear regression
We will then proceed to fit simple regression models. We will begin by fitting what’s known as an empty model to show a key property of linear regression models and then move on to the bivariate regression between pay and working hours.
So let us begin by making sure that we have full information on all cases. Otherwise we cannot compare models in any meaningful way. We will use the complete.cases() to do this

lfs<-lfs[complete.cases(lfs$loghrpay, lfs$ftpt, lfs$tothrs, lfs$class, lfs$age, lfs$sex), ]


5.4.1 The empty model
Now that we understand what the coefficients mean let us fit our first model. This will be an empty or null model, i.e. a model with no independent variables. We do this to highlight that the mean is also a model - a simplified representation - of our data:
\[Y_i = b_0 + e_i\]
This equation states that our DV is equal to the intercept (the sample mean) plus some error - in other words, the mean is an imperfect summary of the data. What this implies is that each of the data observations is equal to the mean plus all the differences between the mean and the actual data.
In a way, we already knew this in the sense from our discussion of the squared errors needed to calculate the standard deviation: If the errors are the data values minus the mean, then the values will be the mean plus the errors!
This is how we specify the model in R:
modelname <- lm (dependent ~ independent, data = dataframe)
In this case we are not including an independent variable, just an intercept (~1) so this should be as follows:

fit0 <- lm(loghrpay~1, data=lfs)
summary(fit0)


Call:
lm(formula = loghrpay ~ 1, data = lfs)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-4.2983 -0.4038 -0.0470  0.3727  3.7044 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 2.401184   0.005681   422.7   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.5603 on 9725 degrees of freedom


This model has only one estimate - the intercept (\(b_0\)):

The intercept is 2.401 with standard error 0.0057 and a very small p-value p<0.001 which is highly significant. Remember that significance in regression is based on a t-test of the null hypothesis that the coefficient is equal to 0.

So the model predicting log hour pay is specified as:
\[\hat{Y} = 2.40\]
Which indicates that the average loghourpay is 2.40. This is an unconditional mean or average, i.e. it is not conditioned, controlled or adjusted for by any other factors.
Indeed if you were to take the mean of loghrpay:

mean(lfs$loghrpay, na.rm=T)

[1] 2.401184


You will get exactly the same: \[\bar{Y} = 2.40\]
In other words, regressing Y without predictors is equal to estimating the mean. Remember that after all, the a property of the mean is that it minimises the errors (total sum of distances between each data point and the mean), which is in essence what the regression line does (albeit with squared residuals).


5.4.2 Model 1: Regressing hourly pay on working hours
This will be our first model that specifically targets our research question by regressing hourly pay on working hours ONLY. This means that the estimated mean working hours is allowed to vary by the number of working hours reported by respondents.
\(Y_i = b_0 + b1 \text{tothrs} + b_2 \text{female} + e_i\)
We can estimate this model in R as follows:

fit1 <- lm(loghrpay ~ tothrs, data=lfs)

And you should obtain the following output:

summary(fit1)


Call:
lm(formula = loghrpay ~ tothrs, data = lfs)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-4.2797 -0.3649 -0.0438  0.3515  3.6275 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 2.0216103  0.0160143  126.24   <2e-16 ***
tothrs      0.0106158  0.0004206   25.24   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.5428 on 9724 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.06148,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.06139 
F-statistic:   637 on 1 and 9724 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Let us describe the intercept (\(b_0\)) and slopes (\(b_1\) and \(b_2\)) in the coefficients section of the regression output.

The intercept \(b_0\) is 2.02 with standard error 0.016 and a very small p-value p<0.001 which is highly significant.
The coefficient \(b_1\) for tothrs is -0.011 with standard error 0.001 and a very small p-value p<0.001 which is highly significant.

So the model predicting log hour pay as a function of working hours is specified as:
\[\hat{Y} = 2.02 + 0.011 \times \text{TOTHOURS} \]
How to interpret this?
Sometimes, the intercept \(b_0\) is tricky to interpret, due to its lack of plausibility. For instance, in this case the intercept would be the mean hourly wages of men who work 0 hours (an out-of-sample prediction, because we only have people who work more than 1 hour).
The tothrs coefficient \(b_1\) capture the raw total effect of working hours on pay. More specifically, that an increase in one hour of work is associated with an increase in log pay of 0.011. From this, we can say that the for each additional increase of one hour worked per hour, the average salary is associated with an increase of 0.011 in log pay.
Now, since interpreting values on log-scale can be unintuitive, we can draw on the following rule of thumb for models where the dependent continuous variable has been log-transformed while the predictors remain in the original units (see this guide for more info). When the DV is on the log scale, we can interpret the coefficients as the % increase in Y associated with one unit increase of x.
\[\hat{Y} = 2.02 + 0.011 \times \text{TOTHOURS} \]
Since \[ b_1 = 0.011 \], this means that for an increase in one hour of work we would expect an increase in pay per hour by a multiple of \[e^{b_1} = e^{0.011} = 1.011061\] - in other words, by 1.1%. Notice that we could also have used the rule of thumb whereby the b1 coefficient times 100 is also 1.1% - \[ b_1 x 100 = 0.011 \times 100 = 1.1\%  \].
This is easier to understand if we plug in values into the equation:
\[\hat{Y} = 2.02 + 0.011 \times \text{tothrs} \]
Let’s compare the average predicted hourly pay of someone who works an 40 hours a week
\[\hat{Y} = 2.02 + 0.011 \times 40 = 2.46\]
with that of someone working the 20 hours a week:
\[\hat{Y} = 2.02 + 0.011 \times 20 = 2.24\]
This means that the difference in (log) hourly pay between a someone working 20 and 40 hours respectively is 0.22:

exp(0.22)

[1] 1.246077


Which indicates that a person working 40h would earn around 25% more per hour than someone working 20 hours. Bear in mind however, that this quite a large difference that is unadjusted by many possible confounding variables and we should expect it to shrink (or attenuate) as a result of controlling for such variables.


5.4.3 Model 2: Regressing hourly pay on full-time vs part-time status
We now re-specify our model full-time vs part-time status. This means that the estimated mean working hours is allowed to vary by whether the respondent is a full-time vs a part-time worker:
\(Y_i = b_0 + b1 \text{part-time} + e_i\)
We can estimate this model in R as follows:

fit2 <- lm(loghrpay ~ ftpt , data=lfs)

And you should obtain the following output:

summary(fit2)


Call:
lm(formula = loghrpay ~ ftpt, data = lfs)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-4.3741 -0.3620 -0.0468  0.3461  3.6285 

Coefficients:
               Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)    2.477024   0.006372  388.72   <2e-16 ***
ftptPart time -0.304552   0.012769  -23.85   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.5446 on 9724 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.05526,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.05517 
F-statistic: 568.8 on 1 and 9724 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


So our model is:
\[\hat{Y_i} = 2.47 - 0.305 \times \text{part-time}\]
Notice here that the intercept has a much more direct and clear substantive meaning - namely, the average log-pay per hour of a full-time worker. This is because the intercept is the predicted value of the dependent variable when the predictor is set to 0. Logically, if part-time is set to 0 and there are only two categories, then it follows tha the intercept represents the average of the reference group (full-time work).
Meanwhile, the \(b_1= - 0.305\) indicates a negative and significant effect of part-time work on pay per hour - i.e. part-time workers earn significantly less per hour than full-time workers. The difference associated with being a part-time worker as opposed to full-time is calculated by exponentiating the \(b_1\)coefficient

exp(0.305)

[1] 1.356625


So \(e^{b_1} = e^{0.305} = 1.357\), indicates that part-time workers received on average 35% lower pay per hour than full-time workers. Again, a very large difference that we would expect to shrink as we control for other antecedent/confounder variables.

title: 5  Linear Regression
text:
5.5 Thinking about confounders
Now, we may suspect that the association between working hours and pay may be the product of other variables that are correlated with both the independent and the dependent variable.
We will consider three key confounding variables or confounders - i.e. variables that are causally responsible for both working hours AND pay, and therefore can partially account for the association between them. In general, we will only control for confounding variables as these are the only ones for which we can be pretty certain that by adjusting for them we will not unwittingly bias the estimation of the effect of interest. In this sense, and for the time being, we should be particularly careful not to control or adjust for intervening or mediating variables (bartram2021?).



Confounding Variables (Source: xkcd)


These are our candidate controls:

sex: Male/Female;
occup: Occupational Class.
age: Age in number of years

And this is how we expect them to be causally related based on relevant academic literature:



Figure 2: DAG for the effect of Working Hours on Hourly Pay Rates adjusted for confounders (Age, Sex and occupation)


Let’s then examine first whether these control variables are indeed associated with working hours and with hourly pay - i.e. that they are potential confounders.

5.5.1 Control 1: Sex
We suspect that both the number of hours worked and pay vary by sex. If this is the case, sex would be a good control candidate variable for our regression model later on.
Let’s examine these bivariate associations:

t.test(lfs$tothrs~lfs$sex)


    Welch Two Sample t-test

data:  lfs$tothrs by lfs$sex
t = 38.326, df = 9724, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group Male and group Female is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 8.990820 9.960067
sample estimates:
  mean in group Male mean in group Female 
            40.59659             31.12115 


As expected, due to the over-representation of women in part-time work, the average number of hours worked is much lower amongst women (30.25) than men (39.81). Indeed, the 95% CI for the difference is between 9.29 and 9.82, which means that we are confident that on the average male worker spends more than 9 hours per week than the average female worker. The t-statistic (t = 70.57) has an associated p-value much smaller than 0.05 so we conclude that the difference is statistically significant.
Notice that looking at the association between working hours measured as part-time vs full-time and sex would also yield a significant association:

This becomes even clearer when we examine the scatterplots again, this time colouring the data points by sex:









We can see how the male data points (red) are over-represented in the longer hours and higher pay, while female data points are over-represented in the shorter hours and lower pay side of the cloud of points. Similarly, we see an over-representations of male workers in higher-paid full-time and an over-representation of female workers on part-time in the mid and low pay. All in all, the bivariate analysis suggests that sex is plausible confounder that we should account for when assessing the association between working hours and pay.


5.5.2 Control 2: Age
We will also consider age as a possible confounder, again following a similar logic and running bivariate tests for all the relevant associations with our main predictor (working hours) and dependent variable (pay).
Let’s see this graphically









So age seems to be positively associated with pay, plausibly the result for job tenure length and work experience, but very weakly, if at all, correlated with age. Let’s calculate the correlation coefficient to find out more precisely:

cor.test(lfs$tothrs, lfs$age, use="complete.obs")


    Pearson's product-moment correlation

This shows that there is indeed a positive significant if weak correlation between age and pay (0.19, p-value<0.0001),and that the correlation between age and total number of hours is significantly different from zero though very weak (0.038, p-value<0.0001).

title: 5  Linear Regression
text:
5.6 Multiple regression

5.6.1 Model 1c: Pay regressed on Working hours + All controls included
Now we will introduce introduce sex, class and age as controls
\[Y_i = b_0 + b1 \text{tothrs} + b_2 \text{sex} + b_3 \text{age} +  b_4 \text{occup} + e_i\]
Be aware though of how categorical predictors in a regression model are actually handled by default in R - i.e. dummy coding. This in practice means that any categorical variable is automatically transformed into a series of binary or dichotomous variables with values 0 (No) or 1 (Yes) representing each one of the categories of the original variable. These are in turn introduced as predictors in the regression model with the first dummy category omitted. This omitted category then becomes the reference category (whose average value of the DV is contained in the intercept or constant), i.e. the category to which the coefficients for the rest of categories are compared. So, for variable sex (male/female) there are 2 dummy variables male (0/1) and female(0/1) where only the second (female) appears in the model; meanwhile, for occupation ( 1 - higher managerial … to 7-routine ) there will be 7 dummies, of which the first will be left out as reference group while the remaining 6 will be introduced in the model. So in practice the model with the main predictor and controls will have the following form:
\[
\begin{split}
Y_i = b_0 + b1 \text{tothrs} + b_2 \text{female} + b_3 \text{age} + \\
b_4 \text{occup2} + b_5 \text{occup3} + b_6 \text{occup4} + \\ b_7 \text{occup5} + b_8 \text{occup6} + e_i
\end{split}
\]

fit1c <- lm(loghrpay ~ tothrs + sex + age + occup, data=lfs)

title: 5  Linear Regression
text:
5.7 Model Fit:
We have already seen in the output that the \(R^2\) was growing as we added new variables. As models become more complex (i.e. as they capture more and more features of the reality we are trying to study) they also explain a greater share of the variance in the DV. It is useful, however, to understand where this \(R^2\) statistic comes from, what does it tell us about our model and how should we use it.
The \(R^2\) is a measure of model fit - i.e. of how well the regression model predicts the data. This statistic is calculated as follows:
\[R^2 = \frac{SS_M}{SS_T} = \frac{\text{Model Sum of Squares}}{\text{Total Sum of Squares}}=\frac{\text{Total Sum of Squares - Residual Sum of Squares }}{\text{Total Sum of Squares}} \]
Let’s begin by explaining the Total Sum of Squares (\(SS_T\)), which you know already from calculating the Standard deviation. Indeed \(SS_T\) is nothing more than the sum of squared differences of the dependent variable Y around the mean \(\bar{Y}\), so it captures the total amount of variation of the variable around the mean
\[SS_T=\sum^n_{i=1}({Y_i-\bar{Y}})^2\]
To understand Model Sum of Squares (\(SS_M\)) is necessary to first make sense of the Residual Sum of Squares (\(SS_R\)). The Residual Sum of Squares is the difference between the predicted values of our dependent variable according to our model \(\hat{Y}\) and the actual observed values of our dependent variable \(\hat{y}\). In other words, it captures the total amount of variation of our dependent variable around the line of best fit or in other words, the inaccuracy of our model.
This is:
\[SS_R=\sum^n_{i=1}({Y_i-\hat{Y}})^2\]
This \(SS_R\) is the value that is minimised in the regression via the method we have been using - i.e. Ordinary Least Squares or OLS regression. So the line of best fit is that which minimises the sum of distances between the data points \(Y_i\) and the predicted values \(\hat{Y}\) define by the regression line.
Finally, the Model Sum of Squares (\(SS_M\)) is the difference between the total sum of squares \(SS_T\) and the residual sum of squares \(SS_R\):
\[SS_M = SS_T - SS_R\]
To understand this think of the following:

The mean is the simplest model of our data, so the total sum of squares tells us how well a model without predictors fits the data
Our model with predictors is a more complex model that captures the data better, so the residual sum of squares should be smaller than the total sum of squares.
The model sum of squares, i.e. the difference between the residual and the total sum of squares, then indicates the improvement in prediction that results from fitting the regression model with predictors in comparison to a model of the mean without predictors.
Thus the \(R^2\) captures the amount of the overall variance in the data that is captured by our model. The larger \(SS_M\) is the greater improvement in model fit have resulted from adding predictors to your model and this will be reflected in a higher \(R^2\).

5.8 Model Diagnostics
For a regression to produce valid estimates of the coefficients there are a number of assumptions that our data and model must meet. Otherwise, there are limits to which you can make inferences about the data and generalise your findings.
These assumptions do not concern the overall fit of the model, but rather how well the model predicts specific observations or range of observations.






Note:


In terms of the code, you can use all the syntax below in your own analysis by just changing the names of the models. So if you have named your model mod5 then you need to replace all the fit2 in the syntax for mod5.




5.8.1 Assessing outliers and influential observations
The OLS regression method assumes that no data points are so large or so small that they influence the estimation of the regression coefficients. If there were extreme values or outliers we should make sure they did not significantly bias the parameter estimates.
We begin by identifying outliers - i.e. cases that differ substantially from the main trend of the data. These are values which are far away from the regression line - they are heavily under or overpredicted - and therefore have very large residuals (\(Y_i-\hat{Y}\)).
To formally identifies outliers we can use the function outlierTest() which runs a Bonferroni Test (a type of t-test). If the p-value is smaller than 0.05 we will consider such observations as outliers:

The next question is whether these outliers affect in any way the regression model - in other words, whether because of their discrepancy with the pattern, they could be shifting the slope and the intercept of our model.
A useful indicator of leverage of a data point can be calculated by checking how the predicted value would change if we moved that point one unit in the vertical (y) direction. This measure would take values from 0 (no effect on the regression model) to 1 (the regression line is forced to go through that point). In R this is achieved with the hat() function the values of which we can plot:

levfit1c <- hat(model.matrix(fit1c))

The plot shows that there is at least one point that is quite far from the main cloud of points, but also that its leverage is quite close to 0 so it does not look as if it could greatly influence our model.
We can also use Cook’s distance to measure influence. Typically, points with a Cook’s distance greater than 1 would require our attention. Let’s do this in R:

Again, we get a similar story with Cook’ distance varying across observations, but on average being quite close to 0.
How is it that our outliers seem to have little effect influence on the model? This is mainly the result of having a very large sample size. The larger the number of observation, the less likely it will be that a single data point can bias the regression estimates.


5.8.2 Normality of residuals
The linear regression model also assumes that the error term in the regression equation is normally distributed. By extension, this means that the regression residuals should also be approximately normally distributed. The easiest way to check such normality assumption is to plot the residuals and inspect them.
We begin by producing a quantile-comparison or quantile-quantile (QQ) plot. This type of graph plots the residuals of your model against the values of the Normal (or the t-distribution). If your model residuals are normally distributed they will largely fall on a straight line. To do this use the qqPlot() function:

# qq plot for studentized residuals
qqPlot(fit1c, main="QQ Plot for Regression Model 4")








66659 72225 
 6402  6975 


You can see that the residuals fall nicely on the straight line for most of the distribution of residuals but that at both extremes the dots representing the residuals begin to move away from the line - downwards at the lowest and upwards at the highest. This means that the distribution of our residuals has slightly heavy tails - the tails have more observations that you would expect if the residuals were truly Normal. You can see this by plotting a histogram of the residuals:

# distribution of studentized residuals
sresid <- studres(fit1c) 
hist(sresid, freq=FALSE, 
     main="Distribution of Studentized Residuals")
xfit<-seq(min(sresid),max(sresid),length=1000) 
yfit<-dnorm(xfit) 
lines(xfit, yfit)








All in all, however, the residuals are distributed approximately like a Normal distibution so our model seems adequate. You should be more concerned if you found that the majority of points do not fall nicely on the line!






Note


If we had not done the log-transformation of our dependent variable we would have had serious issues of non-normality with the residuals that would have made our model problematic. This is why it is so important that we examine the distribution of the dependent continuous variable, and potentially transform it, before we build the linear regression model.





5.8.3 Constant Variance of Residuals
The next assumption our model must meet is that the spread of the residuals has to be constant across different levels of the predicted values. This is known as the “homoscedasticity” or constant variance assumption. The reason why this matters is that if residuals are larger for some predicted values than others, this means that our model is better at describing some parts of the data than others!

# plot studentized residuals vs. fitted values 
spreadLevelPlot(fit1c)









Suggested power transformation:  -0.3394814 


The fact that the line is slightly upwards indicates that there is some evidence that as the values of predicted income (\(\hat{Y_i}\)) increase the variance or spread of residuals also increases. Now, given that the line is not too steep we can still use our findings, but bear in mind that what this plot tells us is that our model predicts the lower earnings with more precision than it predicts higher earnings.


5.8.4 Excessive correlation amongst predictors (a.k.a. multicollinearity)
Finally, we test that our independent variables are not too highly correlated (multicollinearity) amongs themselves. We do this because (a) we want to avoid feeding redundant information into our model and (b) because if two independent variables in a model are heavily correlated they will basically mitigate each other’s effects.
We use command vif() for variance correction factors to check that such correlations are not too large. The VIF is helpful because it gives us a rule of thumb such that any values higher than 2 suggest a possible problem of multicollinearity.

title: 6  Binary Logistic Regression
text:
6.1 Introduction
Many social phenomena are discrete or categorical rather than continuous in nature, and such phenomena are often measured by means of a dichotomous or dummy variable - i.e. categorical dependent variables that can only take 2 values. Indeed in sociology and social policy we are much more likely to deal with categorical than continuous variables (poor vs non-poor, in work vs out of work, graduate vs non-graduate, etc.).
For reasons we will discuss below, the assumptions made by the linear regression model - a.k.a. ordinary least-squares regression (OLS) - are not best suited to handle binary outcomes. To analyse a binary dependent variable as a function of multiple independent variables, we need to specify a regression model in such a way that it takes into consideration the nature of binary variables.
This workshop will introduce you to the foundations and application of such type of statistical model: the logistic regression

text:
6.2 Introducing Logistic Regression
Now that our dataset is ready for analysis, we discuss the logistic regression model. As highlighted earlier, if our dependent variable is categorical and binary, the OLS linear regression model has some issues, so we usually employ a different modelling approach.
There are a number of reasons why OLS regression is inappropriate when using binary DVs, but these reasons are ultimately related to the properties of a variable that can only take two possible values. These reasons can be divided in two types: substantive and statistical

6.2.1 Substantive reason against OLS for binary DV
We need to think differently about a binary dependent variable than we do about a continuous one. In linear regression we model the expected value of a DV (the mean of Y) conditional on the predictors X. This makes sense because we can calculate the mean of a continuous variable, such as income or number of visits abroad in the past 24 months, and measure how it changes for different levels of a variable or type of respondent.
This would not be the case with a binary variable, because the mean of a binary variable (if coded 0 and 1) is actually a proportion of respondents with a value of 1. For instance, you would calculate the proportion of people who are employed or probability that a randomly selected individual will be employed. By definition, proportions and probabilities are bounded by 0 and 1, whereas in theory the mean of a continuous variables can take any value between plus or minus infinity. This is known as the boundary problem, and to understand this it is useful to visualise it.
Let us see what happens when we produce a scatterplot with a binary dependent variable and a continuous independent variable:









As you can see, contrary to the scatterplots you are used to see with two continuous variables, there is no cloud of points but rather two parallel lines of points located at y=0 and y=1.


`geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'









Now, consider a scatterplot with real data: Vote as a DV and Age as a predictor where we overlay a OLS regression line. As you can see the data points are concentrated at 0 and 1 (we have introduced some vertical random noise so that the overlapping points are visible) the scatterplot shows that the dependent variable can only take values 0 and 1.









The line of best fit minimises the squared differences between the predicted values and the observed values. Notice however that the linear regression can, as age increases beyond the original range, predict values that exceed 1, even when the proportions are bound at 1 as maximum value. This is simply non-sensical!
So the main substantive reason why OLS is inadequate for binary dependent variables is that the model can predict values that are essentially impossible. It is important to note here that it is not the binary variable that’s the problem, but that the functional form of our model simply does not fit the data well. In other words, the problem is in assuming that a straight line (the linearity assumption in OLS) provides an appropriate representation of a relationship represent the relationship between a binary DV and IV.


6.2.2 Statistical reasons against OLS for binary DV
There are also more technical reasons why OLS is not appropriate when modelling a binary DV.
The first problem is that the distribution of errors is clearly not Normal. In a linear regression with a continuous dependent variable we assume that the error term (as reflected in the residuals) is normally distributed. This is impossible with a dependent variable because there are only two possible residuals for each value of the independent variable X. This is simply because there are only two possible values (1 and 0) that can deviate from the prediction. Thus:
\[1-\hat{Y}=1-(b_0 + b_1 X_{i}) \quad \text{when} \quad Y_i=1\]
\[0-\hat{Y}=0-(b_0 + b_1 X_{i}) \quad \text{when} \quad Y_i=0\]
The second, more important problem is that the variance of errors will not be constant across different levels of the predictors and/or predicted values - a violation of the homoskedasticity assumption. This becomes clear if you consider the scatterplot we saw early. The residuals (vertical distances between predicted values and observed values) are very small as the line approaches 0 or 1, but anywhere in between the residuals will likely be large (the distance between the points and the line is larger.) This has consequences for the estimation of the standard errors which will be larger and therefore you will artificially need more data to find signicant coefficients.
Summming up, we tend not to use OLS regression with a binary DV because:

the relation is not linear
the model will predict values outside of the 0 to 1 range
the residuals will not be normally distributed
the variance of the residuals will not be constant across different levels of X.

Be aware, however, that in some disciplines researchers may use the so-called Linear Probability Model, which is essentially a linear regression with a binary dependent variable. Generally, the LPM will produce substantive conclusions about the effects of interest that are roughly the same as the logistic regression, even if it will produce implausible out-of-bound predictions. It is important, thus to consider what is the aim of your research when doing the analysis: are you trying to estimate unbiased causal effects? or are you trying to make predictions?

6.3 From contingency table to logistic regression
To understand what the regression logistic is doing with our data it is useful to start with a very simple contingency table. Imagine we are interested in the relation between voting behaviour and wealth. A fair proxy for weight is housing tenure - i.e. whether the respondent is a property owner or a tenant in rented accomodation. Let us first have a look at the univariate distribution of both variables:

#Descriptive stats

##Tables
votetab<-table(bes$vote05)
addmargins(votetab)


Not Voted     Voted       Sum 
     1064      3040      4104 

prop.table(votetab)


Not Voted     Voted 
    0.259     0.741 

tenuretab<-table(bes$tenure)
addmargins(tenuretab)


 Owner Rental    Sum 
  2987   1119   4106 

prop.table(tenuretab)


 Owner Rental 
 0.727  0.273 


And now run a contingency table of vote by tenure:

tenvote<-table(bes$vote05,bes$tenure)

addmargins(tenvote)

           
            Owner Rental  Sum
  Not Voted   583    481 1064
  Voted      2404    636 3040
  Sum        2987   1117 4104

prop.table(tenvote, 2)

           
            Owner Rental
  Not Voted 0.195  0.431
  Voted     0.805  0.569


We can visualise the same information by means of a stacked bar chart:

#stacked bar chart
ggplot(data=bes[!is.na(bes$vote05) & !is.na(bes$tenure) , ], 
       aes(x=tenure, fill=vote05)) +
  geom_bar(stat="count", aes(fill=vote05), position="fill")









6.3.1 Running a chi-squared test of association:
As we discussed earlier a chi-squared test is a hypothesis test that measures the strength of evidence against the null hypothesis.
Remember that the Null Hypothesis states that there is no association between two categorical variables or, in other words, that the distribution of one variable is the same regardless of the category of the other variables. In our case, the null hypothesis is as follows:

There is no association between voting and housing tenure
The distribution of voters and non-voters will be (broadly) the same across owners and non-owners.

We can use the expected and observed values to calculate the chi-squared statistic (\(\chi^2\)). Remember that the formula is as follows:
\[\chi^2 = \sum_{i=1}^{k}\frac{(O_i - E_i)^2}{E_i} \]
This means that the chi-squared statistic is equal to the sum of the squared differences between observed counts (data) and expected counts (null hypothesis) divided by the expected counts.
The larger the value of \(\chi^2\) the greater the difference between your data and what we should expect to see if there were no relationship between the two variables of interest. The second step in the chi-squared tests addresses the following question: What is the probability that the difference between observed and expected is at least as large as that captured by chi^2 if the null hypothesis were true?
In R this is quite easy to reproduce:

#we run a chi-squared test 
chi_tenvote<-chisq.test(tenvote, correct = FALSE)
chi_tenvote


    Pearson's Chi-squared test

data:  tenvote
X-squared = 235, df = 1, p-value <2e-16


In this case, we find a very small p-value indicating that if the null hypothesis were true, the probability of us observing such a large difference between observed and expected values is very small. We then say that there is a significant association between vote and housing tenure.


6.3.2 Odds and Odds Ratio
There is a large and statistically significant difference in the distribution of voters and non-voters across tenure status. On average, individuals who own their home are much more likely to vote than those who rent. But how much more likely are they?
To answer this question we can use a different way of expressing probabilities: the odds. To calculate the odds of an event we divide the probability of an event by the probability that the event won’t occur:
\[O_{event} = \frac{P(event)}{1-P(event)}\]
Let’s look at the table again:

prop.table(tenvote, 2)

           
            Owner Rental
  Not Voted 0.195  0.431
  Voted     0.805  0.569


For instance the odds of a homeowner voting as opposed to not voting are:
\[O_{vote|owner} = \frac{P(vote|owner)}{1-P(vote|owner)}=\frac{0.805}{0.195} = 4.13 \]
And the odds of a tenant voting as opposed to not voting:
\[O_{vote|tenant} = \frac{P(vote|tenant)}{1-P(vote|tenant)}=\frac{0.569}{0.431} = 1.32 \]
Once we have the odds of each event we can compare how likely each event is compared to the other by means of the Odds Ratio (OR) or relative odds which is nothing more than the ratio of two odds. For instance the Odds Ratio of a homeowner voting as opposed to a tenant voting is:
\[OR =  \frac{O_{vote|owner}}{O_{vote|tenant}}=\frac{4.13}{1.32} = 3.12 \]
This indicates that a homeowner is three times more likely to vote than someone who lives in rented accommodation.


6.3.3 Odds to Logits
You may be now wondering how this relates to logistic regression. It turns out that the logistic regression is in essence a linear regression in which the binary dependent variable has been transformed.
Recall that our main problem is that proportions and probabilities cannot exceed 0 or 1, but that the linear regression line can predict values outside that range. What we need is to be able to get rid of these boundaries by transforming probabilities into so-called logits.

The first step is to transform the probabilities into odds. This allows probabilities to be expressed in such a way that they can take values larger than 1 and up to infinite.
The second step is to take the natural logarithm of the odds which gets rid of the 0 boundary so that it can take negative values.

The resulting quantities are the logits or log-odds which are essentially a way of representing probabilities in a way that can be treated continuosly.
\[logit =ln(\frac{p}{1-p})\]
Thus we can specify a logistic regression model that looks like this:
\[ln(\frac{p}{1-p})=b_0+b_1Xi \]

6.4 Specifying a binary logistic regression in R
So let us begin by making sure that we have full information on all cases. Otherwise we cannot compare models in any meaningful way. Since we will use all of the variables in the dataset we can specify

bes<-bes[complete.cases(bes), ]

We specify the first model, which regresses the log-odds of voting on whether the respondent owns the house. The model can be specified formally as an equation:
\[log\bigg(\frac{P(\text{Voted})}{P(\text{Not voted})}\bigg) = b_0 + b1 \text{TENURE}\]

6.4.1 Fitting a simple logistic regression in R:
The basic syntax for a logistic regression in R is as follows:
\[\text{model1 <- glm(DV ~ IV1 + IV2 + ... + IV, data = dataset, family = "binomial")}\]
Before we run the model and interpret coefficients R will produce, consider the following:

The table of coefficients produced by R for a logistic regression has many similarities with the linear regression output.
The dependent variable is the log-odds or logits of an event happening, in our case the transformed probability that a person will have voted conditional on their characteristics as represented by the independent variable.
The coefficients (or estimates as R names them) are thus indicating the difference in logits - i.e. the difference or change in the logit or log odds of an event happening associated with a 1 unit increase in the independent variable (continuous) or with the comparison of one group against another (categorical).
There are no \(R^2\) statistics. It is possible to produce so-called pseudo-\(R^2\) indicators (see later) but they don’t have the same meaning.
There are no F-test statistics of global significance either. We can however compare models against each other and test whether a more complex model provides a significant improvement in model fit.




DAG for unadjusted effect to tenure on vote


So the syntax for our first model is:

model1 <- glm(vote05 ~ tenure, data = bes, family = "binomial")
summary(model1)

Similar to linear regression we pay attention to the estimates and the p-values. In this case we find that the coefficient for being in rented accomodation (tenureRental) is -1.24 with a very small associated p-value. This indicates a negative and statistically significant difference in the probability of voting vs not voting for those who rent as opposed to those who own their home.
We can also transform the logit coefficients into odds-ratio (a different way of reporting the logistic regression coefficients) that (for some) may be easier to interpret:

exp(cbind(OR=coef(model1), confint(model1)))

Waiting for profiling to be done...


                OR 2.5 % 97.5 %
(Intercept)  4.410 3.939  4.951
tenureRental 0.289 0.235  0.355


To understand odds-ratio coefficients here’s a brief introduction:

If the OR are equal to 1 then the probability of experiencing an event is equal for the target group (renters) than for the reference group (voters).
If the OR are larger than 1 then the probability of experiencing an event is greater for the target group than for the reference group. If OR are equal to 1.5 that means that on average the target group is 50% (or 1.5 times) more likely than the reference group to experience an event. If OR are equal to 3 that means that on average the target group is 3 times more likely than the reference group to experience an event.
If the OR are smaller than 1 then the probability of experiencing an event is smaller for the target group than for the reference group. If OR are equal to 0.5 that means that on average the target group is 50% less likely than the reference group to experience an event. You could also say that, conversely, the reference group is twice as likely as the target group to experience the event.

So if the OR comparing the probability of voting between renters to owners is 0.29, all you need to do is subtract than from 1 and you’ll have the percentage decrease in probability associated with such group:
\[1-0.29=0.71\] This means that on average the target group is 71% less likely than the reference group to report being worried.
Alternatively, if you find the “% less likely” wording a bit awkward, you could just always invert the odds ratio:
\[1/0.29=3.45\]
Which means that on average owners are 3.45 times more likely than the renters to vote.


6.4.2 Reporting simple logistic regression:
I have fitted a simple logistic regressio model with “whether or not voted in the General Election” as binary dependent variable and Tenure (owner/renter) as independent variable. The model coefficients show that the log odds of voting are statistically significantly smaller amongst those respondents who rent their homes (b=-1.24, z=-11.8, p<0.001). Expressing the coefficient as odds-ratio, we find that renters are 71% less likely (CI = 64%, 77%) to report having voted in the previous general election than those who own their homes. This confirms our expectation that voter turnout amongst renters is much lower than amongst owners, thus pointing to a possible association between wealth or socioeconomic status and electoral participation.


6.4.3 Fitting a multiple logistic regression in R
Now we add a number of control variables(education, age) that may account for why homeowners are more likely to vote. We do this because we suspect that (a) on average, older people are more likely to both own their home and to vote and (b) the more educated are more likely to vote and to own their home (possibly due to having greater disposable incomes).



DAG for adjusted effect to tenure on vote


Again formally this is:
\[log\bigg(\frac{P(\text{Voted})}{P(\text{Not Voted})}\bigg) = b_0 + b1 \text{TENURE} +  b_2 \text{EDUCATION} + b_3 \text{AGE}\]
And in R this is:

model2 <- glm(vote05 ~ tenure + education + age, data = bes, family = "binomial")

In other words, that even if we hold education and age constant, those who are in rented accomodation are significantly less likely to vote than those who own their property. 6.4.4 Reporting a multiple logistic regression:
I have fitted a multiple logistic regression model with “whether or not voted in the General Election” as binary dependent variable and Tenure (owner/renter), education and age as independent variables. The first thing to notice is that after controlling for education and age the log odds of having voted in the previous general election are still much lower for those who own their home compared to those who rent (b=-0.87, z=-7.62, p<0.001). Expressing the coefficient as odds-ratio, we find that renters are 58% (CI= 47% -76%) less likely to vote than homeowners holding age and educational qualification constant.
Overall, the results of our model suggest that there is indeed a significant and negative relationship between renting and voting behaviour. This association holds even when controlling for age and education.

text:
6.5 Model fit
Now the model fit of logistic regression cannot be evaluated in the same way as OLS. Neither the F-test of global significance or \(R^2\) are available to us to decide whether our model is any good in absolute terms. There are however a number of options that involve the assessment of relative model fit which are discussed below:

6.5.1 AIC
As part of the regression output you obtain an indicator called AIC which stands for Akaike’s Information Criterion. This indicator allows you to compare models against each other to help you decide which is best. The lower the AIC value, the better the model fits the data.
You can either check the regression outputs again or you can retrieve the AICs directly:

model1$aic

[1] 2594

model2$aic

[1] 2413


As you can see model 2 (AIC=2413) achieves a lower AIC value than the first model (AIC=2594) so we conclude it provides a better fit to the data. This should not be surprising as the model has more information (in the form of additional variables) and predicts the data more accurately.


6.5.2 Pseudo-\(R^2\)
There are also a number of indicators called Pseudo-\(R^2\) that try to approximate in logistic regression what the \(R^2\) does for linear regression. These are however not directly comparable to the R-squared for OLS models. Nor can they be interpreted as the proportion of the variability in the dependent variable that is explained by model. Instead pseudo R-squared measures are relative measures of fit, i.e. they compare the fit of one model to that of another model.
The nagelkerke() function computes those for you. By default, it compares the fit of the null model (a logistic regression model with your DV but without predictors) to the model of your choice. Let us do this with the first of our models:

nagelkerke(model1)

$Models
                                            
Model: "glm, vote05 ~ tenure, binomial, bes"
Null:  "glm, vote05 ~ 1, binomial, bes"     

$Pseudo.R.squared.for.model.vs.null

McFadden                               0.0495
Cox and Snell (ML)                     0.0530
Nagelkerke (Cragg and Uhler)           0.0795

$Likelihood.ratio.test
 Df.diff LogLik.diff Chisq  p.value

$Number.of.observations
           
Model: 2478
Null:  2478

$Messages
[1] "Note: For models fit with REML, these statistics are based on refitting with ML"

$Warnings
[1] "None"


The output shows 3 different Pseudo-\(R^2\) measures (McFadden, Cox and Snell, Nagelkerke). From those numbers alone, you cannot conclude anything about how well your model fits the data, only that it fits better than a model without predictors. It includes also the log-likelihood ratio test which is significant. This means that our model with one predictor provides a better fit than the model without predictors.
Now, this on its own does not tell you much. It is only by comparing them to the same measures for a model based on exactly the same data and dependent variable (a nested model) that you can learn something. Let’s run the same command with our final model:

6.5.3 Log-likelihood Ratio Test
We can also make a comparison by testing the null hypothesis that the more complex model is NOT an improvement over the simpler model. If significant we would conclude that the model 2 is an improvement over model 1. It is easy to do this in R using either of the following lines:

anova(model1 , model2, test="Chisq")

The very small p-value suggests that there is a significant improvement in introducing the control variables to our model compared to the first model with only tenure as a predictor.


6.5.4 Classification rate
Another interesting indication of how well our model fits the data is by estimating the classification rate of our model. This means calculating the percentage of cases that our model predicts should be “worried” and “not worried” about cybercrime and comparing it to the actual data. This is achieved by building a contingency table with the cyber variable on the rows and the predicted values on the columns.
Remember however that the predicted values of the logistic regression will be probabilities rather than 0 or 1s, so we need to trick R into transforming values that exceed the 0.5 probability into 1s. This is achieved as follows:

predict <- predict(model2, type = 'response')

accuracy<-table(bes$vote05, predict > 0.5)

accuracy

           
            FALSE TRUE
  Not Voted   138  454
  Voted        82 1804


The diagonal of the table captures the cases that have been correctly classified - i.e. Not Worried & FALSE and Worried & TRUE. While the remaining off-diagonal cells are those cases that the model got wrong. As you can see, many the cases have been classified in the wrong category based on our prediction, so it is useful to know exactly what percentage of the cases our model actually got right. We can find the classification rate by running the line below which essentially sums the cases in the diagonal, divides them by the total sum of cases and multiplies that by 100:

#add the diagonal and divide it by the total
sum(diag(accuracy))/sum(accuracy)*100

[1] 78.4


This tells us that our model correctly classifies around 78% of the observations. This is pretty good considering that we are only working with three predictors - i.e. our model gets just under 22% of the predictions wrong - but yet again we are working with a rather simple and simplistic model. There are many more independent variables we could have included that would make our model fit better and predict our data more accurately!

The short answers is that there is not right or wrong answer as to whether we should keep the variable in the model. It largely depends on the theoretical model you are trying to test. There are however ways to at least evaluate whether the removal of the variable would have a significant effect on the overall model fit.

7.2 What is your estimand?
First and foremost, before you apply a test or specify a regression model, you need to define precisely what is it that you are trying to estimate or measure. This is known as the theoretical estimand or quantity of interest, and it is theoretical because it exists outside of the statistical model(Lundberg et al., n.d.).
The theoretical estimand involves specifying two distinct but, in your project, interrelated things:







Unit-specific quantity
Target population




Effect of marriage on women’s probability of experiencing domestic violence
Married and cohabiting couples (excludes singles, widowed, divorced…)


Effect of living in a former coal area on youth employment chances in Yorkshire
Working age youth in Yorkshire who live in former coal mining areas and those who do not (excludes everyone else)


Effect of having children (mitigation) on sentence length
Court sentences involving time to be served (excludes suspended sentences, fines, …)


Effect of probation on re-offending
Those who have been sentenced for offences that are eligible for probation (excludes very serious offences)



Once you have defined your estimand with sufficient precision the next step is to link it to observable data into an empirical estimand and in turn to an estimation strategy.

title: 7  Model building and Interactions
text:
7.3 Thinking about controls
Suppose then that our estimand is the effect of ideology on attitudes towards the welfare state and that we expect that those located more to the left of the political spectrum are more likely to be supportive of and positive about the welfare state.
To make the claim that ideology causes welfare state attitudes we should be able to show evidence that:

There is an association between the assumed cause and effect
The direction flows from cause to effect
Other explanations are ruled out

The third is the key problem we face with observational data, like that derived from surveys. Unlike in an experimental setting, we cannot randomly allocate people into being left wing or right wing and then compare their views on the welfare state and on the basis of that conclude that ideology has a causal effect on welfare attitudes.
Instead, we need a different strategy for ruling out other potential explanations, one that involves conditioning the effect of ideology on welfare attitudes on a range of variables that could be plausible common causes or confounders of the association between ideology and welfare attitudes.
Now, consider the following candidate variables shown as nodes in the diagram below, draw the arrows or edges that connect them causally and identify which is the main association of interest and which variables act as controls. Make sure that you provide a theoretical rationale for how you have chosen to connect the nodes one way or another.

You should have come up with something like this:

Conditioning (or controlling, or adjusting) requires an appropriate set of controls. The problem is that there is not correct number of control variables that you should include in any model. It should all be derived from substantive knowledge from your research area.

Omitted variable bias is the result of too few controls. This means that you have not been able to rule out that the association is not spurious.

Solution: Think carefully about other common causes both observable and unobservable that could be confounding your target association and try to think of ways in which they could be introduce in your model.

Over-adjustment bias is the result of including too many (and often bad) controls which may well bias your estimates.

Solution: Think carefully whether it makes sense to control for a variable based on your substantive knowledge of the problem you are studying


In general you should always adjust or control for confounding variables (either endogenous or exogenous). These are examples of good controls

Remember that confounders must precede (or at least be concurrent with) the main predictor and be causally responsible for both the main predictor and the outcome/DV.
Avoid however controlling for variables that mediate the effect of interest, as this will tend to introduce a bias in the effect of x on y as it will then be split into a direct and an indirect effect (it will no longer be the total effect).

There are many other types of bad controls, but you will learn more about those in semester 2.

7.4 Building a regression model

7.4.1 Dataset
The variable welfare - a summated scale of welfare related survey items that represents the overall view of respondents on the welfare state. The scale is coded in such a way that the higher the value the more positive the respondent is about the welfare state. The items are as follows:

SBSTREC - SOCIAL BENEFITS/SERVICES PLACE TOO GREAT STRAIN ON ECONOMY
SBPRVPV - SOCIAL BENEFITS/SERVICES PREVENT WIDESPREAD POVERTY
SBEQSOC - SOCIAL BENEFITS/SERVICES LEAD TO A MORE EQUAL SOCIETY
SBBSNTX - SOCIAL BENEFITS/SERVICES COST BUSINESSES TOO MUCH IN TAXES/CHARGES
SBLAZY - SOCIAL BENEFITS/SERVICES MAKE PEOPLE LAZY
SBLWCOA - SOCIAL BENEFITS/SERVICES MAKE PEOPLE LESS WILLING CARE FOR ONE ANOTHER

The second variable we will analyse is a binary variable we will call sblazy2 which is the result of recoding the original five categories of sblazy into two, where the first category is a combination of “Strongly agree”, “Agree” and “Neither” and the second category is a combination of “Disagree” and “Strongly disagree”. The rationale behind this coding decision is that we want to model the probability of having a positive view of the welfare state (as opposed to a neutral or negative one).
We will regress both of those welfare attitudes as dependent variables on the left-right self-placement scales as main predictor. This will take place across two separate models as we have done in past workshops according to the measurement level of the DV.


7.4.2 Preliminary step: Subset complete cases
IMPORTANT: You will only be able to do this after you have selected your independent variables. So once you have a model you are satisfied with you need to select complete cases and run the models again
If regression models are fitted over different datasets, formal and informal comparisons of model fit are strictly speaking not valid. When we fit a model, however, we are only using the cases of respondents who have so-called full information, i.e. individuals who have provided valid answers to ALL the variables included in the model.
In practice by including different independent variables with different patterns of missing data across different models, we end up with models that are based on slightly different datasets. Thus, if we want to meaningfully compare models, we need a dataset that has complete cases for all the variables we are considering.
To do this we use the following command (NOTICE THE COMMA AT THE END!!!) or you could also use drop_na() in tidyverse style.

ess_reg <- ess[complete.cases(ess$welfare, ess$lrscale, ess$cntry, ess$grad, ess$agea, ess$gndr) ,]

What this line does is create a new dataset called ess_reg that includes only those observations that have complete information for every variable we will include in the model.

title: 7  Model building and Interactions
text:
7.5 Interactions

7.5.1 What are interaction “effects” and when should we consider using them in a regression model?
So far, we have specified regression models in which predictors are included additively - i.e. the coefficients add or subtract some quantity from the intercept expressed in the metric of the dependent variable. This means that the independent variables in the model are assumed not to interact in predicting the outcome - hence the ceteris paribus assumption, whereby the coefficients are interpreted as the difference in the DV associated with one unit increase or a change of category in the IV when all other variables are held to be constant.
An important implication of this is that the slope coefficient for any given independent variable is assumed to be equal across the levels the control variables. For instance, if we regress pay on sex and years spent in education we are implying that the differences in pay associated with sex are constant across all ages, or conversely that the association between pay and age is the same for men and women.
This may not be a tenable assumption in many circumstances. Indeed, when independent variables have large main effects, it is highly likely that they will interact to some extent. For instance, since the gender pay gap has a crucial life course component related (though not exclusively) to child rearing and also that, historically, the pay gap has narrowed over time, it seems implausible that the difference in average pay between women and men in their 50s is the same as that for those in their 30s. In other words, we suspect that the association between pay and gender will vary over age groups. These kinds of questions are those that we can assess by specifying interaction terms in our regression models.
Interaction terms are also called multiplicative terms because they are introduced in the regression model as the product of the two variables that are hypothesised to interact in order to produce a significant difference in the expected value of the dependent variable. Interaction terms can be the product of any combination of two or more variables regardless of their measurement level, as shown in the following examples

Categorical x Categorical:

Pay ~ Unionised x Economic sector: We know that unionised workers have on average higher pay than non-unionised workers, but does this pay premium vary across public and private sector workers?
Part-time ~ Gender x Graduate: We know that women are much more likely to work part-time than men, but is the gap in working hours the same for graduate and non-graduates?

Continuous x Categorical:

Attitudes ~ Age x Urban: We know that as people get older they are more likely to oppose same-sex marriage, but is this pattern the same in rural and urban areas?
Vote ~ Income x Country : We know that, on average, higher earners are more likely to vote conservative political parties. Is this association the same in the UK than in Sweden or Spain?

Continuous x Continuous:

Wellbeing ~ Income x local area deprivation: We know that on average people with higher incomes tend to enjoy greater psychological wellbeing, but is that association affected by the level of deprivation in one’s local environment?
Inequality ~ Union density x Leftist Parties vote share: We know that across countries inequality is negatively associated with union density (union membership rates) as their demands often benefit those who get paid less. We may want to know whether this association is unaffected by whether governments are more or less left wing


All these examples suggest that a particular association amongst two variables of interest, represented by its slope coefficient, is also affected or moderated by a third variable. The key to understanding this in a regression context, is that while main effect coefficients add or subtract from the intercept, interaction effects add or subtract from the slope main effect coefficients of each of the interacting variables.Substantively, this means that interaction effects, if significantly different from 0, modify in some way the slope - either by increasing or decreasing its slope gradient or expected difference. If the interaction effect is insignificant, then we can infer that the difference
Some advice:

Specify interaction effects when you have a sound substantive social scientific reason to do so.
Always introduce both main effects as well as the interaction term (for the time being anyway and unless you have a good reason not to)
Make sure you have large sample sizes for the dataset as a whole and also for the groups you are comparing (otherwise you may conclude insignificant results even though the “true” effect is significant).
Some textbooks advise that there is not much point in interacting variables whose main effect coefficients are insignificant or very small on their own. This is however questionable from a causal inference perspective, so take that advice with a pinch of salt and use your substantive judgment.
Unless you center or standardise your predictors (we do not cover this in this module), do not interpret the main effects of the predictors that you have allowed to interact as their interpretation will be affected by the assumption that the interaction is held constant.



7.5.2 Interaction effects in linear regression
After interpreting the regression coefficients, you will have noticed that being on the right of ideological spectrum seems associated with less positive views of the welfare state. You may well suspect, given what we know about cross-national states arrangements that this association may vary across countries (amongst other things because respondents in different countries are being asked to express their views on welfare states that are different). To test that hypothesis as part of the regression we can introduce an interaction term which is the equivalent of multiplying two independent variables together.
In R this is expressed by including a new predictor called lrscale:cntry which will measure how the differences in welfare attitudes across the ideological spectrum vary depending on the country of residence. The interaction effect can, however, also be interpreted as the extent to which the average differences in attitudes between countries vary depending on the respondent’s ideology. Remember, interaction terms are symmetrical, it’s our substantive interpretation that gives them a particular meaning in terms of causal direction.
Here’s the same model as before, now with the interaction term:
